title: The effect of brain-computer interface controlled functional electrical stimulation training on rehabilitation of upper limb after stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Ren, Chunlin; Li, Xinmin; Gao, Qian; Pan, Mengyang; Wang, Jing; Yang, Fangjie; Duan, Zhenfei; Guo, Pengxue; Zhang, Yasu
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Several clinical studies have demonstrated that brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) controlled functional electrical stimulation (FES) facilitate neurological recovery in patients with stroke. This review aims to evaluate the effectiveness of BCI-FES training on upper limb functional recovery in stroke patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Science Direct and Web of Science were systematically searched from inception to October 2023. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) employing BCI-FES training were included. The methodological quality of the RCTs was assessed using the PEDro scale. Meta-analysis was conducted using RevMan 5.4.1 and STATA 18.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The meta-analysis comprised 290 patients from 10 RCTs. Results showed a moderate effect size in upper limb function recovery through BCI-FES training (SMD = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.26–0.73, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.0001). Subgroup analysis revealed that BCI-FES training significantly enhanced upper limb motor function in BCI-FES vs. FES group (SMD = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.00–0.74, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 21%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.05), and the BCI-FES + CR vs. CR group (SMD = 0.61, 95% CI: 0.28–0.95, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.0003). Moreover, BCI-FES training demonstrated effectiveness in both subacute (SMD = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.25–0.87, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.0004) and chronic groups (SMD = 0.42, 95% CI: 0.05–0.78, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 45%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.02). Subgroup analysis showed that both adjusting (SMD = 0.55, 95% CI: 0.24–0.87, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.0006) and fixing (SMD = 0.43, 95% CI: 0.07–0.78, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 46%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.02). BCI thresholds before training significantly improved motor function in stroke patients. Both motor imagery (MI) (SMD = 0.41 95% CI: 0.12–0.71, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 13%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.006) and action observation (AO) (SMD = 0.73, 95% CI: 0.26–1.20, I
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.002) as mental tasks significantly improved upper limb function in stroke patients.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>BCI-FES has significant immediate effects on upper limb function in subacute and chronic stroke patients, but evidence for its long-term impact remains limited. Using AO as the mental task may be a more effective BCI-FES training strategy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Systematic review registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Identifier: CRD42023485744,
                      <jats:uri>https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD42023485744</jats:uri>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
